title: Smart money and dumb money
header_line: My analysis of one book on an entrepreneur's life. Not a summary of the book. Not affiliated with or endorsed by the author or publisher.

lines.text: Who has a say in your business? Did you choose them?

A student asked if voting shares are valued differently. I said no, but they carry votes. If you buy a certain amount of equity, you also buy a seat on the board, and you negotiate for it. The founder can say no.

As entrepreneurs, I said, we have what you call smart money and dumb money. Sometimes the money invested in your company comes from somebody strategic, a mentor, somebody who is going to help you advance the company.
When you take on votes, I said, you need to make sure you value those people.
I gave the example of one of the best-known founders, who took on more money and more shareholders, lost control of the board, and was fired from his own company.

You want a board, I said, because, number one, it gives stability to your business. Number two, it gives investors a safety: it is not just one person making major decisions. There is a board of seasoned people who understand the industry.
So there is a balance, I said: putting together a board of people you can listen to, and losing control of your company, which is the other extreme.

A student asked: isn't it best to own the majority and let people you trust be your board? I said I believe wholeheartedly in having a board of advisors. I love to ask people's opinion, and to get feedback before I make a major decision. That is my personal thing.
I know friends of mine who are comfortable making a decision on their own, I said. So there is a real balance there.

As I retell the chapter, the author was growing fast, from billboards to radio to television in a year, and his conservative board saw all the signs of danger and risk. I said we will see how much he is calculating his risk.
Remember, I said, advertising is the first thing an economy cuts when there is a recession. It is a very vulnerable business.
Who is on your board of advisors?

exercise.title: Five minutes
steps: Write the people whose opinion you ask before a big decision.
Write who gives you more than money or help: a mentor.
Write one person you would not give a vote to, and why.
Write what a board of advisors would help you avoid.
Write one decision you will ask for feedback on this week.

check.q: What did I say smart money is?
choices: Money from somebody strategic, like a mentor, who helps advance the company

check.q: Why did I say you want a board?
choices: It gives stability and safety, so one person isn't making every major decision
It makes the company look big

check.q: What do I like to do before a major decision?
choices: Ask people's opinion and get feedback

recap: Choose who has a say. Take smart money, and keep a balance between advice and control.
